blocks.text: The **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** is the country’s central bank. It was created under the **RBI Act, 1934** and began working on **1 April 1935**, following the recommendation of the **Hilton Young Commission** (the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance, 1926). It started life as a privately owned bank, but since **nationalisation in 1949** it has been fully owned by the Government of India.

blocks.title: Brief history of the RBI
items: Hilton Young Commission reports to the British Government of India and recommends a central bank. Aims: separate the control of currency and credit from the government, and spread banking facilities across the country.
The White Paper on Indian Constitutional Reforms recommends a Reserve Bank; a fresh Bill is introduced in the Legislative Assembly.
The Bill is passed and receives the Governor General’s assent, becoming the RBI Act, 1934.
RBI starts operations as the banker to the Central Government, as a privately owned bank.
Head office shifted from Kolkata to Mumbai.
RBI ceases to be the currency-issuing authority of Burma (now Myanmar).
RBI stops acting as banker to the Government of Burma.
RBI stops providing central banking services to Pakistan.

Government nationalises RBI under the Reserve Bank (Transfer of Public Ownership) Act, 1948, paying compensation to private shareholders; from 1 January 1949 it works as a government-owned central bank. The Banking Regulation Act is also enacted in 1949.

blocks.phrase: Hilton ’26 → Act ’34 → Start ’35 → Mumbai ’37 → Govt’s own ’49

blocks.note: Pair the years as 34-35 (Act, then start), 37 (move), 49 (nationalised). The year 1948 belongs only to the Transfer of Public Ownership Act.

blocks.title: Established vs nationalised
blocks.text: RBI was **established in 1935** but **nationalised in 1949** (1 January 1949). Do not mix them up with 1969 and 1980, which are the years when commercial banks were nationalised.

blocks.title: Accounting year
blocks.text: RBI used to follow a July to June accounting year. From 2020-21 it follows the April to March year used by banks and the government.

RBI’s affairs are run by a **Central Board of Directors** appointed by the Government of India in line with the RBI Act. The board has **20 members** and is appointed or nominated for **four years**. The Governor leads the board, and the four Deputy Governors report to the Governor directly.

blocks.text: The RBI wears seven hats. Each role has its own objective, from keeping prices stable to making sure the public always has good-quality currency.

blocks.title: Seven roles of the RBI
rows: Formulates, implements and monitors monetary policy
Price stability and an adequate flow of credit to productive sectors
Regulator and supervisor of the financial system
Sets broad parameters within which banks and the financial system work
Public confidence, protection of depositors’ interest, cost-effective banking services
Administers the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA)
Facilitate external trade and payments; orderly development of the forex market
Issues and exchanges notes and coins, and destroys those unfit for circulation
Adequate supply of good-quality notes and coins
Performs a wide range of promotional functions
Acts as banker (and merchant banker) to the central and state governments
Handle government receipts, payments and public debt
Maintains the accounts of all scheduled banks
Custodian of banks’ cash reserves; lender of last resort

blocks.title: What the RBI does NOT do
blocks.text: RBI does **not accept deposits from, or lend to, the general public**, and it does not present the Budget or set fiscal policy (that is the government’s job). Overall **monetary policy** is its responsibility, and it is the **banker to the government, not SBI**.

blocks.title: Emblem
blocks.text: The RBI emblem shows a **tiger** standing under a palm tree.

sections.title: Monetary policy tools at a glance

blocks.text: Instruments of monetary policy are the tools the monetary authority uses to reach its predetermined objectives. **Quantitative (general) tools** control the total volume and cost of credit. **Qualitative (selective) tools** steer credit towards or away from particular uses and sectors.

blocks.title: How RBI tightens liquidity
items: RBI raises repo, CRR or SLR
Tools make money costlier or scarcer
Less credit flows into the system
Liquidity in the economy comes down

blocks.note: Add repo, reverse repo, LAF and MSF as the newer quantitative tools.

sections.title: Repo, reverse repo, CRR, SLR, OMO and bank rate

blocks.title: The main quantitative tools
rows: Rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to banks against government securities (a sale of securities with a promise to repurchase at a fixed price). A higher repo rate makes funds costlier for banks, so loans to customers get costlier and less credit flows, which brings liquidity down.

Rate at which the RBI borrows short-term funds from banks by selling them government securities with a promise to buy them back later. Raising it encourages banks to park cash with the RBI, so liquidity in the system falls.
Percentage of a bank’s total deposits that must be kept as cash with the RBI. A high CRR leaves banks less to lend and curbs liquidity; a low CRR does the opposite.

Percentage of deposits (net demand and time liabilities, NDTL) that banks must hold as liquid assets: cash, gold and unencumbered government-approved securities. A lower SLR means more funds to lend. Banks report SLR to the RBI every alternate Friday and pay penalties for any shortfall.

Buying and selling of government securities by the RBI to manage short-term money supply. Buying injects funds; selling absorbs cash from banks. RBI uses it regularly, even outside its policy reviews.

The re-discounting rate at which the RBI lends to banks against bills of exchange, commercial papers and other approved securities. In recent years the repo rate, not the bank rate, guides banks’ own rates; the bank rate follows the repo.

blocks.title: Which way does RBI move the tool?
Current rates as given in the 2024-25 syllabus
Repo vs reverse repo
blocks.phrase: Repo: banks Rent cash from RBI. Reverse repo: RBI Rents (parks) cash from banks.
letters: RBI lends to banks; they repay with interest. Higher repo means costlier loans and less liquidity.
RBI borrows from banks. Higher reverse repo means banks park more cash, so liquidity is absorbed.
MSF = Bank rate, then Repo, then Reverse repo (6.75, 6.50, 3.35 in the snapshot)

blocks.title: CRR vs SLR
blocks.text: **CRR** is kept **as cash with the RBI**. **SLR** is held by the **bank itself** in cash, gold or approved securities. Both are percentages of NDTL, and both are mandatory.

Qualitative tools are used for selective purposes: they regulate the flow of credit and its cost to specific sectors rather than to the whole economy.

blocks.title: The six qualitative tools
rows: The difference between the value of the security offered and the amount borrowed from the bank.
Rules on down payments and maximum maturities of instalment credit for buying goods.
Oral and written statements, appeals, guidelines and warnings issued to banks.
RBI controls the credit granted or allocated by commercial banks.
Psychological and informal means of selective credit control; persuasion rather than orders.
Step taken against banks that do not fulfil conditions: RBI may refuse to rediscount their papers, or charge a penal rate over and above the bank rate for credit demanded beyond a limit.

blocks.title: Soft to hard
blocks.text: Moral suasion and guidelines are the **softest** tools (requests). Direct action is the **hardest** (penalties).

blocks.title: Other important tools
rows: A monetary policy tool that lets banks borrow through repurchase agreements. It helps banks adjust day-to-day mismatches in liquidity and works through the repo and reverse repo windows.
The penal rate at which banks can borrow from the central bank. Announced in the Monetary Policy 2011-12; effective from 9 May 2014. When introduced it was set 1 percentage point above the repo rate.
System under which banks must increase financing of priority sectors such as agriculture and small industries.
Marginal Cost of funds based Lending Rate (MCLR)

New RBI guidelines for how banks set lending rates. It applies to floating-rate home loans and term loans to small and medium enterprises and mid-level corporates, and replaced the Base Rate system from April 2016.

blocks.title: Lending-rate ladder
blocks.text: Lending-rate systems in order: **Base Rate (2010)** then **MCLR (April 2016)**. MSF is a **penal** rate: it sits above the repo rate (6.75% against 6.50% in the 2024-25 snapshot).

The **Monetary Policy Committee** is a committee of the RBI responsible for fixing the benchmark interest rate. It was brought in through an amendment of the RBI Act (the framework dates from 2015) to add transparency and accountability to India’s monetary policy.

blocks.title: MPC facts

By majority; the Governor has a casting vote in case of a tie
4% annual inflation, with an upper tolerance of 6% and a lower tolerance of 2% (the mandate stated in the syllabus ran until 31 March 2021)
At least four times a year

blocks.text: **6 members = 3 + 3**. **4% target, 2% to 6% band.** **At least 4 meetings** a year. The Governor chairs and holds the **casting vote**.

sections.title: Banker to the government and issuer of currency

blocks.text: As banker to the government, RBI receives and pays money for the Centre, carries out exchange, remittance and other banking operations, and manages the public debt of the Union. For states it works under agreements; as per the syllabus such agreements exist with all state governments except Sikkim.

blocks.title: Sections of the RBI Act to remember
rows: RBI must undertake the receipts and payments of the Central Government, and manage the public debt of the Union
State government transactions are carried out under agreements with each state
RBI has the sole right to issue bank notes
Report of the Central Board on RBI’s working is submitted to the Central Government

blocks.title: Currency and government-banking facts
items: RBI issues and exchanges notes and coins and destroys those not fit for circulation.
**One rupee notes and coins are issued by the Government of India**, not by the RBI; the government decides how many coins are minted.
RBI gives **Ways and Means Advances (WMA)** to both the Central and the State Governments.
RBI’s stake in the State Bank of India was transferred to the Government of India.

blocks.title: Who is the government’s banker?
blocks.text: The government’s banker is the **RBI**, even though SBI conducts a lot of government business as an agent.

blocks.title: What happened
items: The government advises the RBI to withdraw the ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes.
RBI’s Central Board meets the very next day and, after deliberation, recommends that the legal tender status of ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes be withdrawn.
RBI reports that 99.3% of demonetised currency has come back: ₹15.31 lakh crore out of ₹15.41 lakh crore.
Household financial savings in currency touch 2.8% of gross national disposable income, the highest in six years.

revision: RBI was set up under the RBI Act, 1934, began on 1 April 1935, and was recommended by the Hilton Young Commission (1926).
Head office: Calcutta first, Mumbai from 1937. Nationalised on 1 January 1949 under the 1948 Transfer of Public Ownership Act.
First Governor: Sir Osborne Smith. First Indian Governor: C. D. Deshmukh. Shortest tenure: Amitav Ghosh (1985).
Central Board has 20 members (Governor, 4 Deputy Governors, 4 Directors, 10 Executive Directors, 1 government official) for four years.
Seven roles: monetary authority, regulator, forex manager, issuer of currency, developmental role, banker to government, banker to banks.
Quantitative tools: bank rate, OMO, CRR, SLR (plus repo, reverse repo, LAF, MSF). Qualitative: rationing, moral suasion, direct action, consumer credit, margins, guidelines.
Repo is the rate at which RBI lends to banks; reverse repo is the rate at which RBI borrows from banks and absorbs liquidity.
CRR is kept as cash with the RBI; SLR is held by the bank in cash, gold or approved securities. Both are percentages of NDTL.
2024-25 snapshot: CRR 4.50%, SLR 18%, repo 6.50%, reverse repo 3.35%, MSF and bank rate 6.75%.
LAF came in June 2000; MSF took effect on 9 May 2014; MCLR replaced the Base Rate in April 2016.
MPC: 6 members (3 RBI + 3 external), Governor chairs with casting vote, 4% inflation target with 2% to 6% band, at least 4 meetings a year, Section 45ZB.
Section 20 covers central government business, Section 21A state business, Section 22 the sole right of note issue.
One rupee notes and coins come from the Government of India, not the RBI.
Demonetisation: advice on 7 Nov 2016, Board met on 8 Nov; 99.3% (₹15.31 of ₹15.41 lakh crore) returned.
UDGAM helps trace unclaimed deposits (10 years); Antardrishti tracks financial inclusion; Utkarsh 2022 is RBI’s three-year strategy.
